beats.say: Two to the power X plus two, times five to the power two X minus one,
asks: What does the question give us?

beats.say: equals five to the power X minus one.
Without a calculator, find the value of ten to the power X.
asks: Do I need to find X?

beats.say: Leave X alone: it is usually an awkward number. Treat ten to the power X as one block.

read: Here $x$ is not a whole number or a simple fraction.
It is about $-0.602$, which we cannot work out without a calculator.
But $10^x$ itself is a simple number.
So we never find $x$: we build $10^x$ straight from the equation.

beats.say: The key fact: ten to the power X equals two to the power X times five to the power X.
asks: Why is ten to the power X two to the power X times five to the power X?

beats.say: Same power, so multiply the bases: two times five is ten.
asks: Does it work for other bases?

beats.say: The plan: put two to the power X beside five to the power X. Then glue them into ten to the power X.
asks: Why do we want them side by side?

beats.say: First, group the fives on one side. Divide both sides by five to the power two X minus one.
Now the twos are on the left and the fives are on the right.
asks: Where did the five on the left go?

beats.say: Same base five, top and bottom, so minus the powers: top power minus bottom power.
Make sure you put brackets, because we minus the whole bottom power.
A common mistake is leaving out the brackets. Then the signs inside come out wrong.
Open the brackets. Minus a bracket flips every sign inside: minus two X, and plus one.

do.text: Minus a bracket flips every sign inside

beats.say: Add up like terms: X minus two X is negative X, and negative one plus one cancels. So five to the power negative X.
Now split the power of two. We want two to the power X on its own, to pair with five to the power X.
Two to the power X plus two is two to the power X times two squared.
This is Add power in reverse: multiplying adds the powers, back to X plus two.
On the right, a negative power flips: five to the power negative X is one over five to the power X.
asks: Why does a negative power flip?

beats.say: Cross multiply: times both sides by five to the power X, so it joins two to the power X.
asks: Why times by five to the power X?

beats.say: On the right, one over five to the power X, times five to the power X, is one.
asks: Why is the right side one?

beats.say: Now two to the power X and five to the power X sit side by side, both to the power X.
asks: Why is side by side useful?

beats.say: They glue into ten to the power X. Same power, so multiply the bases: two times five is ten.
asks: How do they become ten to the power X?

beats.say: And two squared is four. So ten to the power X times four equals one.
asks: Where did the four come from?

beats.say: Divide both sides by four. Ten to the power X equals one quarter.
asks: Can I leave it as a fraction?
What is it as a decimal?
